body.guess: The scheduler is not work-conserving: when UDP's queue is empty because UDP needs less than weightUdp of the link, the scheduler idles or does not give UDP's unused share to TCP, so TCP is throttled by UDP's underuse.
body.unseen: Scheduler idle behavior when the UDP queue is empty; TCP may be served only during the fraction of time when UDP is using its configured share.
body.matters: If true, reducing weightUdp toward UDP's offered load (about 0.3) can remove idle time and raise TCP goodput substantially.
body.reason: A weightUdp sweep can show whether TCP changes when UDP's configured share changes, especially above and below the UDP offered load.
body.observations: E0 (default settings) shows UDP goodput 300003200 bps, essentially the offered UDP rate, with udp_loss_frac=0, drops_band0=0, drops_band1=0, and tcp_retrans=0. TCP goodput is 299885434 bps. link_util=0.618051, so roughly 380 Mbps of the 1 Gbps link is unused even though TCP always has data and there are no drops or retransmissions. The central unexplained fact is why TCP does not use the unused capacity. Two broad possibilities are: (a) the scheduler wastes UDP's unused configured share or otherwise caps TCP, or (b) TCP itself is limited by congestion control, the 1 MB socket buffers, and RTT. A second unknown is the minimum weightUdp that keeps udp_loss_frac <= 0.01; UDP offered load is 300 Mbps, so a byte-rate scheduler would suggest a threshold near 0.3, but the scheduler's exact behavior is not described.

body.result: TCP goodput is about 300 Mbps with no TCP drops or retransmissions.
body.guess: TCP is limited by its 1 MB send/receive buffers and RTT (window-delay product), not by the scheduler; the default TCP rate is already near the maximum a 1 MB window can sustain on this link.
body.unseen: TCP cwnd near the receive-window limit, and queueing/device-buffer delay making the effective RTT large enough that W/RTT is about 300 Mbps.
body.matters: If true, lowering weightUdp alone will not raise TCP much; reducing queueing delay or choosing a congestion-control variant that keeps RTT lower may matter more.
body.reason: The default run's series (cwnd and queue sizes) plus the weight sweep can separate a window/RTT limit from a scheduler limit.

body.unseen: The scheduler serves UDP at approximately weightUdp times the link rate when UDP is backlogged, and UDP queue growth converts a small service deficit into loss over the measured duration.
body.matters: This sets the lower bound for weightUdp; if TCP benefits from lower weightUdp, the best safe setting is likely just high enough to keep udp_loss_frac <= 0.01.

body.because: If the scheduler idled UDP's configured share or failed to give unused UDP share to TCP, tcp_goodput_bps should change when weightUdp changes, and UDP should drop when weightUdp=0.2 because UDP offered load is 300 Mbps. Instead, weightUdp=0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.6 all give about 300 Mbps TCP, 300 Mbps UDP, zero UDP loss, zero drops, empty queues, and the same link utilization.
body.observations: E0 and E1 show that changing weightUdp from 0.2 to 0.6 leaves udp_goodput_bps at 300003200, udp_loss_frac at 0, drops at 0, and tcp_goodput_bps around 300 Mbps; all differences are inside the 1% tolerance. link_util stays about 0.618-0.619, so about 380 Mbps of link capacity is unused. The r001 series shows empty queues, no drops, and cwnd growing from about 0.52 MB at t=1.3 s to about 0.92 MB at t=11.9 s. The implied RTT from cwnd/tcp_bps is about 20 ms, the propagation RTT, so there is no queueing delay. The main unexplained fact is why TCP does not use the spare link capacity: is the default run limited by Cubic's slow cwnd growth over the 10 s measured window, by the 1 MB receive/send buffer ceiling, by the congestion-control variant, or by some scheduler behavior that only appears when TCP becomes larger?

body.because: E1 supports the scheduler-not-limiting part: weightUdp has no effect and queues are empty. The r001 series supports a window/RTT relation: cwnd/tcp_bps is about 20 ms, and cwnd is approaching the 1 MB buffer size. However, cwnd is still growing at the end of the default run, so the exact limiter may be the congestion-control ramp rate rather than a steady-state buffer ceiling. This remains worth testing with tcpVariant and duration.

UDP loss did not appear at weightUdp=0.2, even though UDP's configured share is below its 300 Mbps offered load. With the default TCP load, total demand is about 600 Mbps, below the 1 Gbps link, and the scheduler appears work-conserving, so UDP receives its full offered load. The UDP loss constraint may bind only if TCP can grow enough to saturate the link.

C5 held: BBR_Q4 and BBR_Q1000 both give tcp_goodput_bps=418901197 and udp_loss_frac=0.0. Queue length does not change BBR's goodput, consistent with BBR keeping queues small and not creating queue-induced RTT or drops.

BBR reaches 418.9 Mbps with empty queues, and Cubic's later steady rate is 419.43 Mbps with cwnd 1,051,248 bytes, about the 1 MB buffer divided by about 20 ms RTT. Weight and queue changes cannot raise BBR. This supports a receive-buffer/RTT ceiling, but the ceiling claim still needs to be checked against the untested TCP variants.

body.next: Close H6 and recommend TcpBbr at the default weightUdp, queuePkts, and duration, because it reaches the observed ceiling and was also tested across scheduler and duration variations.
body.observations: E4 and C6 show that, with TcpBbr as the reference at 418901197 bps, none of the remaining tested TCP variants exceeds it by more than 1%: TcpBic is 418510438 bps, inside the 1% tolerance, while TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, and TcpVegas are materially lower. Together with E2 and E3, this leaves no measured setting that raises TCP goodput above about 419 Mbps while keeping udp_loss_frac at 0. The remaining unexplained items are not decision-relevant for the recommendation: duration=2 for BBR was not tested, and seed variation was not tested.

body.because: C6 held: TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, TcpVegas, and TcpBic all stayed within 1% of TcpBbr's 418901197 bps or below it. TcpBbr and TcpBic are effectively tied, and the other variants are lower. This fits the guess that the fixed 1 MB TCP buffer and about 20 ms RTT create a ceiling near 419 Mbps, rather than scheduler or queue settings setting the limit.

body.limit: The result is limited by the fixed TCP socket buffer and round-trip time, not by the scheduler, queue length, or link capacity. TcpBbr reaches about 418.9 Mbps, close to 1 MB divided by about 20 ms, while link_util is only 0.746044 and there are zero drops and zero retransmissions. Changing weightUdp from 0.05 to 0.95 or queuePkts from 4 to 1000 does not change the result, and no tested TCP variant exceeds TcpBbr by more than 1%. Evidence: E2, E3, E4, C4, C5, C6, K4, K8.
body.explanation: TcpBbr is best because it reaches the observed buffer/RTT ceiling within the 10 s measurement. E2 shows TcpBbr gives 418901197 bps at duration=10 and essentially the same value at duration=30, so duration is not limiting for BBR. E3 shows weightUdp=0.05 and 0.95, and queuePkts=4 and 1000, all give the same tcp_goodput_bps=418901197 with udp_loss_frac=0.0, so the scheduler is work-conserving under these loads and queue size does not create meaningful RTT or drops. E4 and C6 show that the remaining TCP variants do not beat BBR by more than 1%; TcpBic ties within tolerance, while TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, and TcpVegas are lower. Therefore the default weightUdp=0.5, queuePkts=100, and duration=10 are kept as the simplest settings, and TcpBbr is recommended because it is at the ceiling and was verified stable across the scheduler and duration variations.
body.holds_when: The UDP application continues to offer about 300 Mbps, the TCP buffers remain 1 MB, the one-way delay remains 10 ms so RTT is about 20 ms, the scheduler remains work-conserving, and total demand remains below the 1 Gbps link capacity. The duration should be at least about 10 s for BBR to be steady.
body.breaks_when: If UDP offered load rises enough that total demand approaches or exceeds 1 Gbps, weightUdp and queuePkts could become binding and UDP loss could appear. If TCP buffers are increased, RTT is reduced, or the scheduler stops giving unused UDP share to TCP, the ceiling or the best weightUdp could change. If duration is made much shorter than 10 s, BBR may not have reached the ceiling.

claims.text: TcpBbr reaches about 418.9 Mbps within 10 s while keeping UDP loss at zero.
For TcpBbr, weightUdp and queuePkts do not materially change TCP goodput or UDP loss over the tested extremes.
No tested TCP variant exceeds TcpBbr by more than 1%; TcpBic is within tolerance and the other variants are lower.
The scheduler and link are not the limiting factor at the recommendation: link utilization is only 0.746044 and there are no drops or retransmissions.
The observed ceiling is consistent with the fixed 1 MB TCP buffer and about 20 ms RTT, not with scheduler share or queue length.

open_questions: Whether TcpBbr at duration=2 would already reach the same ceiling was not tested.
Whether TcpBbr and TcpBic remain tied under different seeds was not tested.
Whether weightUdp or queuePkts become binding if UDP offered load is increased so total demand approaches 1 Gbps was not tested.
